newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian 88 CEO says company not on block.
newsitem.headline: Canadian 88 CEO says company not on block.

text.p: Canadian 88 Energy Corp Chief Executive Greg Noval said on Monday he had been approached by potential suitors, but added the company was not for sale.
Canadian 88 was rumored to be entertaining offers after its failed bid for Morrison Petroleums early this year. Noval denied the reports at the time.

In a terse question and answer session with reporters after Canadian 88's annual meeting today, he said he would reject any offer of C$6 a share, but would consider C$7. "It would be something we'd have to look at -- who makes the offer," Noval said.

"I'd look seriously at any offer, but I guess what I would have to do is stack it up with the growth. If you look at the growth we can create here at Canadian 88, then the company's not for sale at six bucks," he said.
Noval told shareholders he expected major financial and production gains over the next two years on the strength of deep gas drilling in the foothills of Alberta.
He said cash flow per share was projected to climb to C$0.72 in 1997 and C$1.26 in 1998 from C$0.35 in 1996.
Earnings per share were expected to jump to C$0.38 in 1997 and C$0.59 in 1998 from C$0.12 last year.

Natural gas production this year was projected to average 115 million cubic feet a day, up from 56.8 MMCFD in 1996, while oil and gas liquids output was targeted at 4,500 barrels a day, an increase from 2,168 last year, he said.
Noval said the company was on track to drill three additional deep sour gas wells before the end of the year at its much-publicized Waterton play in the southern Alberta foothills.
Waterton's reserve potential after last year's discovery well was estimated at 300 billion-500 billion cubic feet of gas.
He declined to tell reporters the hydrogen sulphide content in the gas at Waterton, opting instead to quote the expected "total shrinkage" at about 35 percent.
Hydrogen sulphide, or H2S, is the "sour" in sour natural gas. Costs of processing rise in proportion with how much H2S is in the gas.
Noval defined shrinkage as H2S content as well as other factors such as the amount of gas used for fuel at a processing plant.

Shell Canada Ltd's Waterton gas plant, where Canadian 88 expects to process its production from the play, can currently take in volumes with H2S content of 30 to 35 percent, Shell Canada vice-president Ron Blakely said.
Noval said Canadian 88 produced gas at its Olds/Crossfield play with H2S content of over 40 percent. "The play...is completely viable or we wouldn't be spending the money we're spending."

He also told shareholders Canadian 88's board of directors was slated to discuss later on Monday whether to distribute the company's 51 percent stake in Prize Energy Inc to shareholders in the form of a dividend.
Canadian 88 shares were unchanged on Monday at 5.55 on the Toronto Stock Exchange.
((Jeffrey Jones, Reuters Calgary Bureau (403) 531-1624))
Two of the C$6-million wells were being drilled, with the first of those currently at the 3,000 metre depth level, about 3/4 of its target depth, he said.

Production from the first well on the play was slated to start producing in September at about 15 million cubic feet a day and development work was scheduled to increase output to 30 million by November, he said.
By next summer, Canadian 88's Waterton gas production was targeted at over 70 MMCFD, Noval said.
